clue.text: First half of Eliot novel in the first person?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the opening word of a two-word George Eliot title, a carpenter's name
second meaning: in Genesis, the first human being created

explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' looks like grammar (I, me) but means the first human in the Bible; the question mark flags that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's novel is titled after a carpenter who shares his name with the first man in Genesis.

clue.text: Harry Styles less content drilling well

indicators.note: a drill bores its way into something, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: hale means healthy, in good health

indicators.note: the contents of a word are its inner letters, so taking them away leaves only the outside pair

parts.note: just the first and last letters of the singer's surname

explanation.surface: Pop star Harry Styles, minus anything worthwhile to say, is digging into a well.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Styles reads as one name, but Harry is the verb defining the answer and Styles is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to pester or torment them repeatedly, and to hassle is the same nagging persecution.

clue.text: Large bed: article carried by everyone round building

indicators.note: in a down clue whatever is carried sits on top of its bearer, so this piece comes first

parts.note: the indefinite article
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
a berth is a bed on a ship or train
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A big bed with something being carried by everyone around a building, like a removal job.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Albert Hall is a circular concert venue in London. 'Large bed' reads as one thing, but splits into a size letter and a sleeping place.
explanation.definitionFit: London's famous concert venue in Kensington is built on an oval, rotunda plan, so it is a round building.

clue.text: Cause of stiffness in lead taps

parts.note: the lead in a show is its star
the two taps on a basin are marked C (cold) and H (hot)

explanation.surface: Something wrong with the lead plumbing makes the taps stiff to turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the metal of old pipes, but it is the main role; taps give their two labels rather than a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch is applied to collars and shirts when laundering to make the fabric rigid and crisp.

clue.text: Small round object is very sharp

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
round as in 'about', which is circa, abbreviated CA
an object is a thing

explanation.surface: A tiny ball turns out to be extremely sharp, perhaps a hazard underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small round object' paints a ball, but round here means approximately, as in 'round about ten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scathing criticism is harsh and cutting, so a very sharp remark or review earns that description.

clue.text: Daydreamers gather this court official's back

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Idle dreamers collect something belonging to a law-court official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court official' reads as one legal figure, but court is a verb for romancing and official only lends its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom wool-gathering means daydreaming, so absent-minded dreamers are said to gather this fibre.

clue.text: One with weight put on, after capital Italian food

indicators.note: in a down clue something put on another lies above it, so it is written first
following something means coming later in the line, so this goes behind what follows

parts.note: Riga is the capital of Latvia
a ton is a unit of weight
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone who has gained weight after eating Italian food in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weight put on' suggests getting fatter, but it places a unit of weight above the numeral; the whole pairing then follows a Baltic capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigatoni is a ridged tube-shaped pasta, a staple dish of Italian cuisine.

clue.text: Guides in uniform and that lady upset me

parts.note: Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U
she is the pronoun for that woman

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters run bottom to top

parts.note: in a crossword, 'me' is the setter who wrote it

explanation.surface: Uniformed guides and some woman have annoyed the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guides in uniform' looks like a whole definition (Girl Guides), but uniform is the letter U. Me as the setter is a common crossword self-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Usherettes are women who show cinema or theatre patrons to their seats, guiding them through the dark.

clue.text: DHL disheartened about unskilled kind of delivery

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps another
losing heart means losing the middle, so only the outer letters survive

parts.note: the courier's initials without the central letter
a raw recruit is untrained or unskilled

explanation.surface: A discouraged courier firm grumbles about an amateurish parcel delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: With a courier firm in the clue, 'delivery' suggests parcels, but it means a manner of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawl is a slow, lengthened way of speaking, so it is a style of vocal delivery.

clue.text: Detective's receiving boost investigating faults etc

indicators.note: whatever receives something takes it inside itself

parts.note: tec is short for detective, plus the S of the possessive
a tonic gives a lift or boost

explanation.surface: A detective gets a lift while looking into people's failings.
explanation.walkthrough: Faults look like human flaws under investigation, but they are geological fractures in the earth's crust.
explanation.definitionFit: Plate tectonics is the branch of geology that studies the crust's structure, including faults, folds and plate movement.

clue.text: Erroneously catch some hoodlum — is he arrested?

indicators.note: only some of the following text is used, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, two whole words, and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A gangster may have been caught in error; is he now under arrest?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' suggests an arrest, fitting the hoodlum, but it means hearing what someone says.
explanation.definitionFit: To mishear is to hear wrongly; catching a word is idiomatic for hearing it, so catching erroneously fits.

clue.text: Preparing the ground in time, I'm going to get older

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
I'll, the contraction of I will, with the apostrophe dropped
to age is to get older

explanation.surface: A gardener digging the soil in good time muses about growing old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In time' looks like a phrase meaning eventually; in is just the link and time a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tillage is the ploughing and cultivating of soil before planting crops, which readies the earth for sowing.

clue.text: Kid might utter one line, boring Trump

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: to trump is to beat
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A child might come out with a dull line about the US president.
explanation.walkthrough: The kid is a young goat, not a child, and 'one' belongs to the definition. Trump is the card-game verb, not the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleat is the cry of a goat or sheep, so a young goat might let out one.

clue.text: Crickets played with this individual little flower on edges of dewy shrub

parts.note: a bud is an unopened flower

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its outermost letters, the first and the last

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
holly is an evergreen shrub

explanation.surface: Insects hop about a single small flower on a dewy bush.
explanation.walkthrough: Crickets look like insects in a garden, but The Crickets were the backing band of the 1950s rock'n'roll singer.
explanation.definitionFit: The American rock'n'roll star fronted a band named The Crickets, so he was the person they played alongside.

clue.text: Mixture of ethanol is in a drop of the hard stuff?

definitions.text: a drop of the hard stuff

indicators.note: a mixture blends its ingredients together, so the letters get stirred into new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cocktail containing alcohol hides inside a dram of strong spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A drop of the hard stuff' is slang for a shot of spirits, which the ethanol encourages; here it is literally a hard drop falling from the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Hail falls as pellets of ice, so each pellet is a frozen solid drop of precipitation.

clue.text: Concealing nothing, almost get angry and violent

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to seethe is to get angry, here with its last letter cut
rough play is violent

explanation.surface: Someone holding nothing back nearly loses their temper and turns aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealing nothing' sounds like honesty about feelings, but describes fabric you can see through.
explanation.definitionFit: Transparent material hides nothing behind it, which is what see-through clothing or glass is.

clue.text: One may care for canines barking in lengthiest day

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and crazy letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog-sitter looks after barking hounds all through the longest day.
explanation.walkthrough: Canines and barking conjure dogs, but canines are pointed teeth; barking is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A hygienist cleans and looks after patients' teeth, and canines are the pointed teeth beside the incisors.

clue.text: European wearing nothing indecent in the shade

indicators.note: in a down clue the wearer sits beneath what it wears, like a head under a hat

parts.note: nil means nothing
E is the abbreviation for European
blue jokes or films are indecent

explanation.surface: A naked European behaving improperly while lounging in the shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the shade' sounds like out of the sun, but shade is the definition, a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Nile blue is a pale greenish-blue colour named after the river, so it is a shade or hue.

clue.text: People who break forcefully into others' addresses?

definitions.text: People who break forcefully into others' addresses?

parts.words: People who break forcefully into others' addresses?
parts.note: surface reading: burglars smashing their way into people's homes; setter's reading: addresses are speeches, and these people loudly interrupt them

explanation.walkthrough: An address is a home but also a formal speech; breaking in is burglary but also interrupting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hecklers shout rude interruptions at speakers during their speeches, cutting in forcefully on what they say.

clue.text: University head's covering security devices

parts.note: Yale is an American university
locks are the hair covering a head

explanation.surface: A university principal is protecting the campus security equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'University head' looks like a vice-chancellor, but head's covering is hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is a brand of cylinder door lock, so these are mechanisms that keep doors secure.

clue.text: Cross after student's expelled for ridicule

indicators.note: someone expelled is thrown out, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a saltire is an X-shaped cross, as on the Scottish flag
L for learner, a student

explanation.surface: A teacher grows cross after a pupil is thrown out for mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' wants to be angry (IRATE, which nearly fits); it is a noun, the diagonal cross of St Andrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire uses mockery, irony and exaggeration to expose folly, so it is a form of ridicule.

clue.text: Decaying matter Mike extracted from dip

indicators.note: something extracted is pulled out and taken away, leaving the rest

parts.note: hummus is a chickpea dip
Mike is the NATO alphabet word for M

explanation.surface: A man named Mike pulls rotting stuff out of a dish of dip.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike looks like a person, but stands for one letter of the NATO alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Humus is the dark organic soil material formed when leaves and plant remains decompose.

clue.text: Servants carrying paper — Times is something on hand

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: men as in servants or staff
the i is a British daily newspaper
T for time, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Servants bring in the newspaper; The Times is always to hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Paper and Times look like one newspaper; they are two pieces, a British daily called i and a doubled abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitten is a glove without separate fingers, so it is literally worn on your hand.

clue.text: Kind of road test including some information

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam
a bit is a small unit of information

explanation.surface: A driving test that covers a bit of theory about the rules of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Road test' suggests a driving exam; the test is a spoken one. An orbital is a British ring road, such as the M25 around London.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbital road circles a city, so it describes a type of highway built as a ring.

clue.text: Picked up tea and rum for really bad hairdresser

indicators.note: to pick something up is to hear it, so the word gives a letter that matches its sound

parts.note: the letter T is said exactly like the drink
rum is old British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: Someone collects tea and rum for a terrible hairdresser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink beside tea, but means strange. Sweeney Todd, the demon barber of Fleet Street, murdered his customers.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional barber killed his clients and had them baked into pies, so he is a murderously bad one.

clue.text: What Napoleon stands on is tail of desert rat?

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a rat and a rotter are both a contemptible person

explanation.surface: Napoleon's stand compared to a Desert Rat, a British soldier of the North African campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon looks like the French emperor but is the pig who rules Orwell's Animal Farm.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's foot is called a trotter, and the boar in Orwell's novel walks on four of them.

clue.text: Gospel needs no introduction — it's part of the Bible

indicators.note: with no introduction there is no opening, so the first letter goes

parts.note: gospel truth: something stated as gospel is the truth

explanation.surface: The Gospel is so famous it needs no introduction, being part of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: Gospel points at Matthew, Mark, Luke or John, but here it means truth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Ruth is a short Old Testament book, so it is one section of scripture.

clue.text: Returned outfit from Madrid without reporting to cleaner

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps round another
something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Real Madrid is the Spanish football club, an outfit being a team
if you report to a boss you work under them

explanation.surface: Clothes brought back from Madrid without being reported to the dry cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outfit' suggests clothes beside a cleaner, but it is a football team; without means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A launderer washes and presses clothes or linen professionally, which makes them a cleaner by trade.

clue.text: For eavesdroppers, supposed one receives hospitality

indicators.note: eavesdroppers only listen, so what matters is how the word sounds

parts.note: supposed means guessed, which is pronounced identically

explanation.surface: Eavesdroppers assume someone is being entertained by their hosts.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone works on the past tense of guess, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest is a visitor who is entertained, fed or housed by a host.
